D009-D008_h001.question:
It’s been a rough year. Most days I just feel low, like there’s this heaviness I can’t shake. Things I used to enjoy—working the fields at sunrise, having tea with my wife, even playing with the grandkids—feel empty. I go through the motions, but it’s like nothing touches me. My mind tires out fast; if I try to work on the accounts or plan the planting, my head feels drained within minutes and I just stare at the page.

I catch myself thinking a lot that it’d be easier if I just wasn’t here. I don’t have some big plan or anything, but the thought “what’s the point, maybe it’s better if I’m gone” keeps coming back.

Earlier this year there was a month where I was the complete opposite. I barely slept—maybe three, four hours—but woke up buzzing with energy, not tired at all. I’d rush from one task to another, pacing if I had nothing to do, fiddling with my hands, unable to sit still. My mood swung fast: one moment joking and feeling on top of the world, the next snapping at my wife over nothing. I talked so fast my family kept telling me to slow down, saying they couldn’t keep up. It didn’t really stop me working, but they were worried, said I wasn’t myself.
D009-D008_h001.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder
D009-D008_h001.answer: C & B. Bipolar II Disorder & Bipolar I Disorder

D009-D008_h002.question:
It’s been a strange couple of years. For most of this past year, I’ve felt weighed down, like there’s a heavy blanket over everything. I used to be so proud of my students and the work I did, but now even when my husband or former colleagues mention achievements or invitations, I just feel…nothing. I don’t care if I finish anything, and even simple things—taking a shower, making breakfast—feel exhausting. I spend a lot of time sitting in my chair, thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up. I catch myself thinking, “I wish I could just disappear,” or “Maybe everyone would be better off without me,” though I haven’t made any plans.

But about a month not too long ago, I was completely different. I was bursting with energy—cleaning the whole house at 2 a.m., starting new projects, reorganizing old lesson plans, calling friends. My mood would flip from feeling on top of the world to snapping at my husband over nothing. I hardly slept for several nights in a row and didn’t feel tired. I talked nonstop, jumping from idea to idea, pacing around the house, wringing my hands if I tried to sit still. It didn’t exactly ruin anything, but it was…a lot, even for me.
D009-D008_h002.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder
D009-D008_h002.answer: C & B. Bipolar II Disorder & Bipolar I Disorder

D009-D008_h003.question:

D009-D008_h004.question:

Outside of work I mostly go straight home. I dodge messages, ignore invitations, let friendships fade because I just don’t have it in me to engage. It’s like I’m watching my own life from a distance. Sometimes, when I’m walking over a bridge or waiting near a busy road, I’ll get this sudden, almost physical urge to just step off or step out, even though I don’t have a plan or actually want to die. It scares me.

But about a month ago, everything suddenly flipped. I started feeling unbelievably good for no clear reason—energized, almost buzzing. I barely sleep now, maybe a couple of hours, but I don’t feel tired. At work I can’t sit still; I’m pacing between stacks, starting multiple projects at once, reorganizing things that don’t really need it. I’ve also been way more focused on sex than usual—constantly thinking about it, texting people late at night, hooking up more than I normally would. It feels exciting and “right” in the moment, but then I look back and wonder if I’m going too far. I’m still managing to show up and do my job, but I can tell something about the way I’m acting isn’t my normal.

D009-D008_h005.question:
